Horseman
HORSS-man
noun
From horse and man, rendering the Hebrew pārāsh — a rider, and by extension the mounted arm of an army, the cavalry that ranked with the chariot as the terror of ancient war.

Biblical Definition

A horseman is a mounted soldier, and in Scripture he is almost always a picture of the strength of the nations — swift, costly, terrifying, and useless against God. Egypt is the first great cavalry power the Bible shows us, and the Bible shows her drowning: “the horse of Pharaoh went in with his chariots and with his horsemen into the sea, and the LORD brought again the waters of the sea upon them” (Exo 15:19). That deliverance set the doctrine for ever after. Israel was forbidden to multiply horses, and Isaiah pronounced the woe when she went shopping for them: “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 31:1). David had already put the whole matter into a line a child can carry: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). Yet the word has a glorious other side. When Elijah was taken up, Elisha cried after him, “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof” (2Ki 2:12) — naming one praying prophet as worth more to the nation than all its cavalry. The true strength of a people is the men who stand before God for it.

Webster 1828 Definition

A rider; a mounted soldier; the cavalry arm of an ancient army.

HORSEMAN, a rider on horseback; a man skilled in riding; a soldier who serves on horseback.

From horse and man; Hebrew pārāsh, a rider or cavalryman.

The mounted arm ranked with the chariot as the chief military strength of the heathen nations.

Israel's kings were forbidden to multiply horses (Deu 17:16); Egypt's horsemen drowned in the sea.

Elisha calls Elijah himself the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof (2Ki 2:12).

Key Scripture

Exo 15:19 — "For the horse of Pharaoh went in with his chariots and with his horsemen into the sea, and the LORD brought again the waters of the sea upon them; but the children of Israel went on dry land in the midst of the sea."

Psa 20:7 — "Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God."

Isa 31:1 — "Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!"

2Ki 2:12 — "And Elisha saw it, and he cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no more: and he took hold of his own clothes, and rent them in two pieces."

Modern Corruption

The horsemen are gone; the trust in visible strength is not, and every age names its own cavalry.

expand to see more

No one now goes down to Egypt for horses, but every generation finds a mounted arm to lean on, and the church is not exempt. The modern horsemen are the platform, the funding, the political majority, the celebrity endorsement, the technology that promises reach without holiness. Isaiah's woe is not aimed at chariots as such; it is aimed at the look. Judah “look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD” — the eyes went where the strength appeared to be, and the strength that was really there went unconsulted. That is the sin, and it is committed as easily in a boardroom as in a stable.

The recovery is not asceticism about means but a fixed order of trust. Psalm 20 does not say the godly own no horses; it says they do not trust them. The believer may plan, build, budget, and arm, and still say with David, “we will remember the name of the LORD our God” — and the proof of which way the heart leans comes on the day the horses are taken away. So Elisha's cry stands as the standing correction: the real cavalry of a nation is the man who prays and preaches and will not bend, and when God removes such a man, the defence is gone though every stable is full. “An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength” (Psa 33:17).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Horseman = a rider, a cavalryman; Hebrew pārāsh, the mounted arm of a host.

expand to see more

Horseman — horse + man; Hebrew pārāsh, a rider.

With the chariot, the chief military strength of Egypt, Syria, Assyria, and Babylon.

Israel's king was forbidden to multiply horses to himself (Deu 17:16).

Pharaoh's horsemen went into the sea and did not come out (Exo 15:19).

Elisha names Elijah the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof (2Ki 2:12).

Usage

"Some trust in chariots, and some in horses — and every age has its own cavalry."

"Isaiah's woe falls not on the horses but on the look that goes to them instead of to God."

"One praying prophet was the chariot and horsemen of a whole nation."
